text.p: Saab Automobile AB Chairman and Chief Executive Robert Hendry on Tuesday said the Swedish automaker had set a goal of achieving profitability in 1998 and showing "acceptable returns" by 2000.

Hendry, speaking to reporters at the North American International Auto Show in Detroit, said the profit goals were linked to Saab's plans to increase annual worldwide sales to 150,000 cars by 2000, from about 99,000 in 1996.
General Motors Corp and Sweden's AB Investor each own 50 percent of Saab.

Hendry said a big slice of the projected sales increase would come from the introduction of a upscale model to replace the Saab 9000 in the United States. The new car, code-named 640, will be produced in Sweden. Its introduction is slated for later this year, with a station wagon version to follow in early 1998.
Hendry said Saab would continue to produce the 9000 for European markets for at least two years and perhaps as long as four years.
Saab also plans to introduce several high-performance versions of its mainstay 900 model in the next two years.
